item.title: Why Your Brain Keeps Replaying Conversations at 2 A.M.
item.description:
Default Mode Network

Why Your Brain Keeps Replaying Conversations at 2 A.M.

Your brain isn't trying to torture you. It's trying to teach you.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Your brain replays situations because it is trying to prepare you for the future, not simply relive the past.
  • Uncertainty keeps social interactions mentally active long after they are over.
  • Transforming thoughts into reflection can reduce anxiety and strengthen resilience.

It's 2:17 a.m., and your brain has decided it's time for some serious self-reflection.

Not about tomorrow's meeting or that never-ending to-do list you will face in the morning, but about a conversation you had with a friend three days ago. All of a sudden, the exact words you used during this conversation are echoing through your mind.

You replay a joke that didn’t land. You remember the awkward thing you said and wish you could have changed it somehow. You remember the meeting where you should have spoken up.

Interestingly, each time your brain plays back that memory, it feels helpful, almost like another rehearsal of the conversation might change it somehow.

But it never does.

Most people assume this is anxiety or simply overthinking, but psychologists have a different view. Your brain is not trying to rewrite the past. Your brain is trying to prepare you for the future and to learn from past experiences to make better future decisions (Nolen-Hoeksema et al., 2008).

This distinction changes everything.

Your Brain is a Prediction Machine

We typically think of memory as a filing cabinet. It’s a place where we store memories of things that have already occurred. Neuroscientists see memory somewhat differently. Memory is one of the most useful predictors of what will happen in the future for the brain. When our brains calculate how to make better decisions, they will go back into previous experiences (Raichle, 2015).

Each of those awkward or bad interactions becomes another piece of data. Every uncomfortable experience becomes information. Every social faux pas becomes another rehearsal for the next time you have a conversation with a friend.

Your brain asks, "What happened? What did I miss? What can I do differently next time?"

Your brain is not trying to embarrass you or keep you awake at night; instead, your brain is trying to train you.

Why Some Conversations Refuse to End

Almost a hundred years ago, psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik made an interesting observation at a café: the waiters there had excellent memories for customers who had unpaid orders, but when a customer paid their bill, the details of the order would disappear from the waiters' minds.

This observation was later termed the “Zeigarnik effect,” which refers to the tendency to have unfinished tasks remain active in our minds because we want to complete them (Zeigarnik, 1927).

Think about an awkward conversation. When you don't know if someone misunderstood you, are concerned about having offended them, or feel like you lost out on an opportunity, your brain leaves that encounter open and unfinished, and continues cycling back to that moment over and over again because unresolved experiences consume our attention (Zeigarnik, 1927).

So your brain keeps going back to that moment.

Again.

And again.

Why Everything Gets Louder at Night

When we rest, the default mode network (DMN) in the brain is working harder than ever. This network is responsible for supporting our memory, self-reflection, the creation of imaginary situations, and creating mental simulations of what may or may not happen in the future (Raichle, 2015). Think of it like your brain's planning committee that meets overnight to get ready for the next day.

The primary purpose of the DMN is a noble one.

The DMN wants to learn.

The DMN wants to help you improve.

However, the DMN will occasionally forget to clock out.

The DMN generates repetitively negative thought patterns (also known as rumination) and is often associated with anxiety and emotional distress due to its ability to focus on issues rather than solutions (Nolen-Hoeksema et al, 2008).

A Hopeful Way Forward

When the mind replays a conversation at two in the morning, try not to listen to it again. Instead, ask a different question:

What can I learn from this situation?

Write down your answer.

Expressive writing research supports that by writing, you can better process emotions by organizing them into a structured thought pattern through the written word (Pennebaker & Smyth, 2016). By writing the experience down instead of just continually replaying what happened, your mind can start to view the situation as a completed experience rather than as a lingering experience.

This change encourages psychological detachment; rather than focusing on the negatives, your brain can shift its focus toward the lesson learned, thereby engaging in reflection rather than rumination, which increases resilience, emotional regulation, and problem-solving skills (Watkins, 2008).

By writing down the lesson learned, you allow the Default Mode Network (DMN) to suspend its constant search process, as writing helps close the loop, completing the task of identifying potentially useful information for future use.

Be thankful for the insight learned and use the moment of writing to let go of previous regret.

Hope isn't believing you will never say the wrong thing again. Hope is trusting that one imperfect conversation cannot define your future. Because growth doesn't come from perfect words. It comes from taking the time to learn long after a conversation ends.

item.title: How Does Music Evoke Emotion?
item.description:
Emotions

How Does Music Evoke Emotion?

The psychological and neurological reasons why music moves you.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Emotion is a fundamental aspect of musical experience.
  • Music has the capacity to mimic emotions.
  • Musical emotion is one of the primary motives for engaging in music listening.
Source: New Africa/Shutterstock/AI Edited

Music helps us step past our rational mind and get in touch with the emotional life we often keep hidden. Music is remarkable in its ability to evoke profound emotions (chills and thrills) in listeners. We often describe pieces of music as sad, joyful, tender, or harsh. The most common motive for listening to music is to influence emotions (Juslin, 2019). How does listening to music produce emotions and pleasure in listeners? The following describes key features of music that explain our emotional responses to music.

  1. Musical pleasure

The key reason people listen to music lies in the reward center of the brain. Listening to pleasurable music activates areas of the reward system. The same brain system that enables feelings of pleasure from sex, recreational drugs, and food is also critical to experiencing musical pleasure. Musical pleasure arises when a pattern is interrupted in some way. Listeners experience strong emotions when something unexpected happens. For example, a listener may expect a dissonant chord to resolve into a consonant one. But this may be delayed by a creative composer to enhance emotional excitement. However, listening to a familiar song holds no surprise, because it is predictable.

  1. Nostalgia

Nostalgia is the most frequent emotion evoked by music. Many listeners use music to remind themselves of valued past events. Listening to music that was played a lot during a significant life event (e.g., a family celebration or teenage years) can trigger a deeply nostalgic emotional experience. The feeling is not the music, but in what it reminds us. For example, we hear certain kinds of music as sad because we have learned to associate them with sad events like funerals.

  1. Rhythm

Rhythm can have a powerful effect on movement because the auditory system has a rich connection to motor systems in the brain. These connections help explain why music often makes us want to dance, and why we feel natural to tap along with music. For example, sounds that are loud and fast-paced generate increases in arousal. In contrast, relaxing music can reduce feelings of anxiety.

  1. Music mimics emotions

Music embodies expressive qualities like melancholy and cheerfulness. For example, a slow tempo naturally conveys sadness, because it has a structural resemblance with the slowness that we might expect in a sad individual. The rapid, skipping tempo, or the loud level of sound, makes music cheerful.

  1. Emotional contagion

Music doesn’t only evoke emotions at the individual level, but also at the interpersonal level. When people attend concerts, their emotions are in part influenced by the emotions of other people present. When sports fans sing together, their brains release oxytocin, which makes them feel an emotional bond with those in their group. That is why nations have national anthems.

  1. Visual imagery

Listening to music provides a great opportunity for daydreaming (Margulis, 2026). For instance, imagining monsters during fear-evoking music enhances fear responses. Imagining nature, such as mountains or fields, enhances our emotional responses to music such as the Four Seasons by Vivaldi. In a high-tech digital age, for some listeners, the easy country melody is a reminder of the ‘good old days.’ Listening to music is a kind of trip that transports us to some other world.

  1. Aesthetic emotion

Aesthetic emotions are typically sought and savored for their own sake. We listen to music to take great pleasure in its beauty. Aesthetic emotions include feeling moved, awe, wonder, transcendence, and tenderness. Aesthetic emotions do not require us to act; they just invite us to savor (Winner, 2019). In response to these emotions, we may experience goosebumps and motivation for the improvement of self and society.

  1. Pleasurable sadness

Sad music evokes a special emotion that people enjoy listening to (Huron, 2011). Listening to sad music can purge a negative emotion, without actually experiencing the loss. Listening to a sad song while in a sad mood is like someone (a friend) empathizing with your experience. It can bring comfort by making us feel connected and that we are not so alone.

In sum, music can inspire emotions. The emotional power of music is one of the main motivations why people devote so much time, energy, and money to it. Music can be used to create an emotional atmosphere such as calming, relaxing, playful, sincere, or intimate. These factors also explain an important emotional benefit of music for mood regulation.

item.title: A Chronic Cough, Anxiety, and an Overlooked Cause
item.description:
Health

A Chronic Cough, Anxiety, and an Overlooked Cause

This one question revealed the cause of a dry cough mystery.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Persistent physical symptoms—for example, a chronic dry cough—can cause anxiety and depression.
  • Before treating anxiety and depression, it is important to find the cause of the persistent physical symptom.
  • A common class of medications can trigger persistent dry cough months or even years after treatment begins.
  • Careful medication review can solve medical mysteries and prevent misdiagnosis.

Sometimes physicians encounter symptoms that remain unexplained despite extensive testing. When no clear medical explanation is found and symptoms persist, patients often develop anxiety and/or depression as a consequence of living with an unresolved health problem.

In such situations, treatment frequently focuses on the emotional consequences while the underlying medical mystery remains unsolved.

Yet occasionally, the right question can reveal a surprisingly simple explanation—and an equally simple solution.

Linda had a persistent dry cough at night.
Source: Chris Gilbert, MD, PhD with ChatGPT.

Case study: A chronic cough

Linda was 54 years old when she came to see me with a persistent dry cough that had lasted 14 months.

The cough was relatively mild during the day but became relentless at night. She described a constant tickling sensation in her throat. Coughing would briefly relieve the sensation, but within seconds, the tickle would return, triggering another coughing spell.

She tried drinking cold water, warm water, and various home remedies, but nothing provided lasting relief. The chronic cough disrupted her sleep night after night, leaving her exhausted during the day.

As the months passed, Linda became increasingly anxious and depressed.

Apart from her cough and being treated for high blood pressure, she was healthy, exercised regularly, and ate a balanced diet.

Linda had never smoked and had no history of asthma. Her physical examination was normal. Blood tests and chest X-rays were unremarkable.

Over the previous year, she had consulted several specialists.

An ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialist performed a laryngoscopy to investigate the throat irritation but found no abnormalities. There was no inflammation and no evidence of postnasal drip.

One internist suspected gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), reasoning that stomach acid might be irritating her throat at night. Linda was prescribed a proton pump inhibitor for three months, but her symptoms remained unchanged.

Another physician worried about the possibility of early lung cancer and ordered a chest CT scan. The scan was normal.

Fourteen months after the cough began, Linda was still suffering.

Because no explanation had been found and her anxiety and depression were worsening, she was about to be referred to a psychiatrist when she came to see me.

The question that solved the mystery

The most important question turned out to be surprisingly simple:

“What medications are you taking?”

When I reviewed Linda’s medications, I discovered that she was taking an ACE inhibitor to treat her high blood pressure.

Suddenly, everything made sense.

The likely culprit was the medication itself.

What research shows

Linda’s experience is far from unique.

ACE inhibitors (angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors), a widely prescribed class of blood pressure medications, are known to cause a chronic dry cough in approximately 5 to 25 percent of patients. The side effect appears to be more common in women and nonsmokers. The cough may begin shortly after treatment starts, but it can also appear months or even years later. [1] [2] [3]

The simplest way to confirm the diagnosis is to discontinue the ACE inhibitor and substitute another class of blood pressure medication. In most patients, the cough improves within days to a few weeks. If the culprit medication is restarted, the cough frequently returns. [4]

Interestingly, this side effect is not usually dose-dependent. Even low doses can trigger coughing in genetically susceptible individuals. [5]

Research suggests that ACE inhibitors lower the threshold of the cough reflex in sensitive patients. As a result, ordinary environmental stimuli that would not normally provoke coughing can suddenly trigger persistent symptoms. [6]

What happened to Linda

I discontinued Linda’s ACE inhibitor and replaced it with a calcium channel blocker, a different class of blood pressure medication.

Within one week, her cough disappeared.

For the first time in more than a year, she was able to sleep through the night. As her sleep improved and her physical symptoms resolved, her anxiety and depression gradually disappeared as well—without the need for psychiatric medication.

Her blood pressure remained well controlled.

The psychological lesson

Linda’s story illustrates an important principle in both medicine and psychology.

When symptoms remain unexplained, it can be tempting to focus solely on treating their emotional consequences. Yet anxiety and depression are often understandable reactions to persistent physical symptoms. Whenever possible, it is important to identify and address the underlying cause rather than treating only the consequences.

Before concluding that a symptom is unexplained or untreatable, clinicians should carefully review all prescription medications, over-the-counter products, and supplements. Sometimes the answer is hiding in plain sight.

Throughout my career, I have encountered numerous patients with chronic dry cough who were treated with allergy medications, acid-reflux therapies, and other interventions while the true cause—an ACE inhibitor—went unnoticed. In some cases, the medication was hidden within a combination blood pressure pill, making it even easier to overlook.

Medicine is both a science and an art. Laboratory tests and imaging studies are invaluable tools, but careful listening and thoughtful questioning remain equally important.

Sometimes the key to solving a medical mystery is not ordering another test—it is asking one more question.

item.title: The Mania Felt Like Clarity
item.description:
Mania

The Mania Felt Like Clarity

Personal Perspective: The danger about mania is that it feels like being chosen.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Our culture prizes manic energy as genius and productivity—a myth that tells the sick that illness is a gift.
  • Recovery can feel like a loss: People often grieve the false clarity and certainty that mania provided.
  • Mania's first casualty is the capacity to truly see another person; it is often the last thing to return.
Source: Alexey Baikov/Pexels

For weeks before everything came apart, I did not so much sleep as pause. I would lie down and rise three hours later, convinced the hours had been wasted, that the world had accelerated and I was keeping pace with it, ahead of it, while everyone around me trudged through fog. Ideas arrived faster than I could write them down. Connections lit up everywhere. A stranger’s glance was a signal. My own thoughts, ordinary for nearly 40 years, had become, overnight, the thoughts of someone chosen.

What most accounts get wrong: It did not feel like sickness. It felt like health. It felt like the best version of myself, finally unleashed.

And there was a seduction in it for someone like me. I had spent my adult life in the profession of thinking, a historian trained to doubt. Mania offered the opposite: not just certainty, but the sense of being inexhaustible and prolific, the energy our culture prizes. The anthropologist Emily Martin, in her study Bipolar Expeditions, describes that energy as “a valuable resource in the ever-accelerating spiral of productivity.” Who, having chosen the life of the mind, would not want to be utterly certain of his own—and inexhaustible besides? It felt like arrival, like becoming, finally, the thinker I was always meant to be.

That is the cruelty of mania, and the reason it is far more dangerous than the sadness we picture. Depression announces itself. The sufferer knows something is wrong and wants it to stop. Mania does the opposite. It feels like a gift. And so the person in its grip becomes its fiercest defender, the last one who will agree to make it stop.

I know, because I was. When the people who loved me began to suggest that something was wrong, I did not laugh it off. I came after them.

The psychologist Xavier Amador gave his book on this reflex the perfect title: I Am Not Sick, I Don’t Need Help! But my defiance was stranger than denial. When my mother said the word mania to my face, I did not flinch—I agreed, proudly: “Yes, this is mania, and you all need to accept it.” The diagnosis was not an accusation to deny but a crown I refused to take off.

Jonathan Lear once described psychoanalysis as “the history of a series of battles that are fought and refought within the human soul.” I have come to picture my own illness as one such battle—a war between two parts of one person, the mind and the soul. I don’t mean these in any religious sense. By the mind, I mean the deterministic engine: the part that calculates, races ahead, wins rooms. By the soul, I mean the moral undercurrent, the seat of conscience and tenderness, the part that can be moved by another person and knows the difference between being clever and being good.

A healthy life keeps these two in conversation. Mania ends the conversation. It hands the whole house to the mind, which, left unsupervised, is dazzling—genuinely dazzling, which is the problem—but has no patience for doubt and no ear for the people who love you. It will charm them, then discard them as obstacles. The soul, meanwhile, gets exiled to some far room of the self where it cannot be heard. It is still there. It is simply outvoted.

In my case, the mind’s weapon of choice was the letter. I wrote long, certain, wounding ones that took petty grievances and inflated them into matters of high principle. The illness took my years as a human rights scholar and bent my faith in speaking truth to power into a righteous crusade against the people closest to me: family who, I had decided, did not love me enough; friends who were envious of my powers or only wanted to control me; colleagues conspiring to keep me down. Every cruelty felt, as I committed it, like courage.

We don’t make this easy because we are half in love with mania as a culture. Martin also recounts how the psychiatrist Ronald Fieve praised what he called mania’s “Midas effect”—its gift for risk, energy, and sweeping others along. He meant it admiringly. But Midas turned everything he loved to cold gold and starved at his own table. We tell the same story in gentler forms: the tormented genius, the doomed artist. There’s a sliver of truth in it, but it is an alluring myth that tells every sick person the most dangerous thing they could hear: that the illness is an innate endowment, and getting well means going dim, the loss of one’s anointed status.

Source: NASA Hubble Space Telescope/Unsplash

A supernova is the most brilliant event in the life of a star—and it is the star destroying itself. The brightness and the catastrophe are the same event. That is mania exactly. People will tell you that you “weren’t yourself.” The harder truth is that you were a self, just a self with the wrong part in charge, burning the rest for fuel.

When the lithium began to work, and the world stopped lighting up with meaning, I grieved. I missed it. I missed feeling chosen. For a while, recovery felt less like healing than like a demotion: being handed back my ordinary mind and ravaged life and told to be grateful.

What I understand now is that the clarity was the lie, and the quiet is the truth. The medication did not dull me. It cleared the room enough that the soul could be heard again—and the soul had been right about nearly everything the mind had been certain of.

The psychiatrist Elio Frattaroli, in Healing the Soul in the Age of the Brain, writes that “it is primarily in our awareness of feeling, not thinking, that we can discover who we really are.” Mania is thought to be at its most certain and least true. The people I’d discarded were not obstacles. The stranger’s glance contained no hidden message. The genius was insomnia, and adrenaline wearing a crown.

Real clarity is far less thrilling than its counterfeit. It does not feel like being let in on a secret. It feels like being able to sit across from my mother and actually see her—not as a character in my drama, but as a person with a life as real and as weighted as my own. That is a type of seeing the manic mind cannot do, for all its brilliance. It was the first thing I lost, and the last thing to come back.

If you have loved someone in the grip of this and watched them defend the very thing destroying them, I hope it helps to know the defense is not stubbornness. It is seduction. What you can do is refuse to be dazzled alongside them, and refuse to turn away—to keep faith with the quiet self still waiting, outvoted, in the far room, for the noise to end.

But faith is not a plan, and it shouldn’t have to be enough. Staying takes more: knowledge that the illness never volunteers, support that no one can shoulder alone, and help that our systems rarely offer freely. How families do that—not how they feel, but what they need—is where these letters are going next.

item.title: Emotional Flooding: When Feelings Take Center Stage
item.description:
Emotions

Emotional Flooding: When Feelings Take Center Stage

Why strong emotions can overwhelm us and how to regain clarity

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • Emotions are protective signals, often shaped by early life events.
  • Anger, shame, guilt, anxiety—one emotion can cascade into the next and overwhelm the nervous system.
  • Emotional flooding can distort the perception of reality.
  • Naming, grounding, and reframing the interpretation of reality can create space between feeling and reaction.
Emotional Flooding
Source: Simaran Sood / Unsplash

Ever been hijacked by an emotion you never saw coming? One moment you feel calm and clear. Then something small happens: a text that goes unanswered, a critical comment from a colleague, an unexpected bill that feels like the last straw. And before you realize it, you’re no longer reacting to an event. You are flooded with anxiety, anger, sadness, or shame.

In those moments, your emotions become the lens through which you filter reality. The feeling becomes the fact, making you react not to the situation itself, but to what the emotion tells you it means, which is rarely the same thing. And often one emotion spills into the next, each one pulling you further from solid ground.

Why Escalation Happens So Fast

Sarah had been looking forward to dinner with her mother for weeks. She’d chosen the restaurant carefully, hoped the evening might feel different this time, warmer, more connected. Within minutes of sitting down, her mother made a comment about the menu. A small remark that, in another context, might have meant nothing. But here it meant everything for Sarah.

After a few more digs, her initial mild irritation turned into red-hot anger. Sarah felt her jaw tighten, her responses shorten. By the time the main course arrived, she made an excuse and left.

In the car, something shifted again. The anger suddenly dissolved, and in its place came shame. Then guilt. Then a spiral of anxious questions she couldn’t stop.

“Did I overreact? Did I just make everything worse? What if she never understands me?”

Within the space of one dinner, Sarah had traveled through four distinct emotional states. And yet, as overwhelming as every single one of those emotions was, each of them was trying to help her.

Emotions Aren’t the Problem

Many of us grow up being told, or simply learning, that strong emotions are a problem to be managed, controlled, or pushed through. But emotions are not design flaws; they are often protective mechanisms that function to alert us to something important and mobilize a response.

Anxiety scans for potential danger before it materializes. Anger activates energy when a boundary is crossed. Sadness slows you down so you can process loss. Guilt prompts you to repair and respect relationships. Shame attempts to prevent rejection by pulling you inward and out of sight.

These are generalizations, of course; emotions are complex and don’t always follow a neat script. But broadly speaking, they are organized survival strategies.

Where it gets complicated is that many of these patterns were shaped early in life, often in environments that weren’t safe or predictable. When, as a child, your safety is put into question, the nervous system learns to constantly scan others for potential threats: a shift in tone of voice, a subtle facial expression, a silence that feels slightly different. Over time, the system stays on alert even when no actual threat is present. What once helped you adapt now keeps you reactive.

Emotions Feel True, but They Aren’t Always Accurate

One of the most important distinctions we can make is between emotional truth and factual truth. Emotions are real. They are powerful. They are undeniable as experiences. But they are not always accurate reflections of what’s actually happening.

When anxiety is running the show, the world looks unsafe. When anger takes hold, everything feels disrespectful or unfair. When sadness moves in, the future can seem sealed shut. And when shame is activated, it can feel as if something is fundamentally broken in who you are. These are not factual observations, but emotional interpretations, shaped by past experience and survival learning. Yet, they are delivered with the certainty of fact.

And when you fully identify with the emotion and accept its interpretation as the whole truth, conscious judgment is the first thing to go. The flood doesn’t just overwhelm you; it convinces you of a verdict that is almost always more damning than the reality.

Three Steps Toward Steadier Ground

The goal of this three-step process is not to eliminate emotions or suppress them. Suppression tends to increase internal pressure over time, making emotional reactions stronger rather than weaker (Gross, J.J., 2001). What you aim for is to change your relationship with your emotions and to become someone who can feel deeply without being swept away, who can be moved without losing their footing.

1. Name what’s happening.

Instead of becoming the emotion, begin to notice it. Rather than thinking, “I am angry,” try “a part of me feels angry right now.” Instead of “I am anxious,” try “a part of me feels unsafe.” This shift creates space between you and the emotion. You’re no longer fully fused with it; you’re observing the feeling as you experience it, and that small gap is where conscious choice becomes possible.

2. Ground yourself in the present.

Emotions tend to pull attention toward imagined futures or unresolved pasts. Grounding returns awareness to the present moment: noticing your feet on the floor, your breath moving in and out, the concrete details of your surroundings. The goal isn’t to eliminate the feeling, but to remind your nervous system that right now, in this moment, it is manageable (Pruessner, 2024).

3. Challenge the certainty.

Emotional flooding feels conclusive; it tells you exactly what is happening and what it means. But these are interpretations, not facts. This is where you become the calm, reassuring presence your younger self may not have had (Gross, J.J. & John, O.P., 2003). Instead of automatically believing the emotional story, you pause and ask:

What else might be true here? What would I tell a close friend in this situation? What is the most compassionate and balanced way to see this?

The goal is simply to see the situation more clearly than your flooded nervous system can manage alone.

Becoming Your Own Steady Presence

The more you practice these three steps, the earlier you catch the emotional flooding before it takes over. You begin to recognize the patterns, the familiar trigger, the chain of emotions that follows. And slowly, you start to meet each emotion with curiosity and clarity rather than alarm.

Of course, strong emotions will still arise—anger, sadness, anxiety, guilt, and shame—some days more forcefully than others. But at some point, you can feel the emotions without becoming them. You can acknowledge what they are trying to protect, ground yourself in the present moment, and see the situation you are in more clearly.

And in that moment, the emotion no longer controls what happens next. Instead of reacting automatically, you have the space to make a conscious choice about how you want to respond.

item.title: Are You Living From the Neck Up?
item.description:
Authenticity

Are You Living From the Neck Up?

Kierkegaard’s guide to the true self.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • The self is not what you have; it is the relationship you have with yourself.
  • Living only “from the neck up” disconnects thought from embodied experience.
  • Success can hide despair when identity depends on status, titles, or approval.
  • Authenticity begins when you stop performing and start becoming who you are.
Source: PeopleImages / Shutterstock/ AI Edited

In our hyper-connected, metrics-driven world, it is easier than ever to mistake our profiles for our personas. We polish our resumes, check our engagement statistics, and cultivate digital identities designed to project achievement. But beneath this surface of curated success, a deeper psychological question looms: Who are you when the audience goes away?

Over a century and a half ago, the Danish existential philosopher Søren Kierkegaard diagnosed the exact anxiety that haunts the modern psyche. In his masterpiece The Sickness Unto Death, he gave a famously dense definition of what it means to be a human being:

"The self is a relation which relates itself to its own self, or it is that in the relation that the relation relates itself to its own self; the self isn’t the relation but that the relation relates itself to its own self."

At first glance, this sentence requires a few rereads. But unpack it, and you find a profound psychological roadmap for genuine mental well-being.

The Mind-Body Split: Living From the Neck Up

To Kierkegaard, the human being is a tension—a relation—between the body and the mind (or soul). Crucially, the "self" is not just the fact that you have a mind and a body; it is the active relationship you maintain with that connection.

Many of us live almost exclusively "from the neck up." We reside in our thoughts, our anxieties, and our cognitive plans, only noticing our feet when they hurt or our bodies when they break down. Kierkegaard’s definition challenges this fragmentation. He suggests that selfhood is an ongoing, embodied feedback loop. To have a healthy self is to be fully present to how your mind and body cohere, balancing your immediate physical reality with the continuous flow of your psychological life.

The Sickness of Success and the Fear of Ourselves

When we lose touch with this internal relationship, we fall into what Kierkegaard calls "despair"—the true "sickness unto death."

Psychologically, this often manifests as an obsessive attachment to external markers of identity: job titles, social prestige, wealth, or relationship status. Kierkegaard could be notoriously harsh toward those who built their lives entirely on social importance. To him, the despair people feel when they lose a corporate title or a prestigious position is shallow, because it reveals a terrifying truth: without the title, they are forced to sit alone with themselves.

And most people, Kierkegaard noted, are deeply afraid of themselves. It is far easier to pursue a demanding career, polish a social media profile, or Google your own name than it is to look inward and ask: Why do I desire what I desire? Am I living a life that is truly mine?

Relieving Existential Guilt Through Passion

When we abandon our authentic potential to fit a standardized social ideal, we develop a chronic, underlying existential guilt. This is not a pathological guilt to be medicated away; it is a sign of "bad faith"—the psychological toll of selling out who we could become for the sake of who society wants us to be.

Kierkegaard’s antidote is a radical return to subjectivity and passion. When he famously declared that "subjectivity is truth," he wasn't advocating for selfishness or narcissism. True subjectivity means taking life—not yourself—seriously. It means acknowledging your past (your constraints, your privileges, your choices) while remaining passionately open to the future.

Ultimately, Kierkegaard reminds us that we cannot find a master plan for life before we start walking. The existential challenge is to cultivate the attention required to face life with dignity, to drop our vanity, and to become worthy of whatever happens to us.

item.title: The Person You’re Talking to Might Not Exist
item.description:
Projection

The Person You’re Talking to Might Not Exist

What a quiet 1979 film taught me about how we invent the people around us.

Posted June 12, 2026

Key points
  • We rarely see people as they are; we see the story we’ve built about them.
  • Projection can be flattering, not just unfair—we hand people wisdom or warmth they never claimed.
  • Because of naive realism, our interpretations feel like plain fact, which makes them hard to catch.
  • The aim isn’t to stop projecting but to notice it, by asking what we’re adding to what we see.

It took me about 90 seconds to decide who he was.

A new colleague, first meeting. Something in the way he ran the room—didn’t smile, answered a question a beat too fast, held eye contact a little too long. Arrogant, I thought, and the verdict closed before I’d heard him say anything that warranted it. For months afterward, I related to that version of him. Polite, guarded, faintly cold. I was careful around a man I had essentially invented.

He wasn’t arrogant. He was terrified. He’d walked into that job convinced everyone in the building was smarter than he was, and the things I’d read as arrogance—the speed, the unbroken eye contact—were the posture of someone bracing for exposure. I hadn’t been reading him at all. I’d been reading a character I cast in a role, and then quietly resenting him for playing it.

I only have language for what I did because of a film I saw far too young to understand.

The film is Being There. Peter Sellers, 1979. Subtle humor, almost no action, long pauses, a strange, gentle current moving underneath everything. Many people watch it now and shrug; it isn’t paced for us. It doesn’t shout or chase your attention. It asks you to sit still long enough to notice what’s happening inside you while you watch. I saw it as a kid and didn’t understand what I understood. I only knew it landed. It took me decades to name what it had done: it showed me, before I had any words for it, how much of what we call perceiving other people is really just our own mind talking back to us.

The premise is almost absurd in its simplicity. A man named Chance has lived his whole life as a sheltered gardener, knowing little beyond his plants and his television. Through a series of accidents, he’s deposited into the world of wealth and power, and the people there begin to hear him as profound. He says something plain about a garden, and a room full of sophisticated people receives it as a parable about the economy. He isn’t trying to deceive anyone. He doesn’t manipulate or perform. He simply exists, and the world does the rest.

Because the real story of the film isn’t what happens to Chance, it’s about what happens to everyone around him. They take a few data points and build a wise man. Then they talk to the wise man they built—not to the person actually standing there.

Psychologists have a name for the trap underneath this. It’s sometimes called naive realism: the deep, mostly invisible conviction that we see the world and the people in it as they truly are, rather than through a lens shaped by our own assumptions, moods, and needs. We don’t experience our interpretations as interpretations. We experience them as simply what’s there. That’s what makes the whole thing so hard to catch. The story we’re telling about a person doesn’t feel like a story. It feels like reality.

And we do it constantly. We do it in relationships and families, at work and online, with strangers at the next table and with the people we claim to know best. We rarely listen to people. We listen to our story about people—our biases, our hopes, our fears, our hunger for someone who confirms that the world makes sense.

What unsettled me, watching the film again as an adult, is that it doesn’t let you stay above it. You start asking the same question the characters ask. Is Chance wise? Innocent? Empty? Enlightened? An accidental saint? And then you catch yourself doing the exact thing the movie is about. Wait—am I projecting onto him right now? That’s what good art does. It doesn’t hand you the lesson. It sets a small trap for your mind and then shows you your own footprints.

There’s a final scene that people have argued about for decades. Chance walks out across the surface of a pond, and the film holds the moment just long enough to make you ask whether you’re watching a miracle or a trick of perspective—or one last joke designed to test how badly you want to turn him into something more than he is. The movie refuses to answer. It just watches you watching.

What I took from it, in the end, was one of the most useful questions a person can carry: What am I adding to what I’m seeing? Not what is happening. Not what is true. What am I adding?

When you can catch what you’re adding—the bias, the backstory, the hunger, the resentment, the hope—something loosens. You don’t have to abandon judgment. You hold it more lightly. You start to notice that your certainty about a person is often a costume your mind puts on because uncertainty feels too exposed.

There’s an uncomfortable flip side, too. Projection isn’t only unfair; sometimes it’s generous. Sometimes the person we project onto benefits—gets swept into a flattering story that hands them wisdom, warmth, or authority they never claimed. Projection can even feel like love. It’s just love aimed at a version of someone that lives inside our own head.

Which is why the goal was never “stop projecting.” You can’t. The mind builds these models faster than you can supervise it. The work is quieter than that: to notice. To catch how fast you decide who someone is. To feel the moment you turn a human being into a symbol. To recognize, now and then, that you’re not looking at the person in front of you at all—you’re watching your own internal movie playing on top of them.

It eventually changed something with that colleague. Not because I became wise about people, but because one day I caught the movie running. I noticed I had a fixed character where a person should have been, and I got curious instead of certain. The terror beneath the “arrogance” was visible almost immediately, once I stopped narrating and started watching.

Some things don’t reach you because they’re exciting. They reach you because they’re true. And sometimes you only understand what you saw the first time when you come back to it years later—carrying enough of your own mistakes to finally recognize yourself in the mirror it was holding up all along.
